paras: The lynching of William Martin was the killing of a Black man near Rome, Covington County, Alabama, in late summer 1888, after he was taken from a deputy sheriff who was moving him to Florida. Martin, accused of assaulting a white woman, was shot and his body thrown into an old well, and the story ran as a brief wire item in Georgia and Kansas papers.

According to a special from Rome relayed through Montgomery, Martin was accused of a "brutal assault" on Mrs. McClellan, whom the dispatch called "a respectable white lady." The dispatch described the assault only as recent and gave no date or details of it.

A "posse of citizens" captured Martin, but, in the dispatch's words, he "had to be shot down before he would surrender." After he partly recovered from his wounds, he was turned over to a deputy sheriff to be taken to Florida. Before he crossed the Alabama line, he was taken from the officer, his body was "riddled with bullets," and he was thrown into an old well.

The report did not name the people who took Martin from the deputy or say how many there were. It also said, without naming a source, that he had made "a full confession" and meant to kill the entire McClellan family.
No report of an inquest, arrest or official response appears in the coverage.

The Atlanta Constitution printed the story on September 11 as one paragraph in the Alabama part of its state-news roundup, between a railroad death and a murder confession. Two days later the Emporia Weekly News in Kansas ran the same Montgomery dispatch, dated September 5, under the headline "A Brutal Negro's End."

Both versions presented the assault and the confession as facts and described the killing as Martin's "horrible" or "terrible" fate, giving no criticism of the killers. The two printings differ only in small points, such as the spelling "McLellan" and "the officers" for "the officer" in the Kansas text.

reader.title: Lynching of William Martin
bases: A Black man accused of assault was taken from a deputy sheriff while being moved and shot to death, his body thrown into a well (A1, A2).

Martin was taken from an officer and his body 'riddled with bullets' in retaliation for an alleged assault (A1, A2), but the report uses the passive voice and never says who took him or how many there were, so a group of three or more is not stated.
Both printings carry the same Montgomery dispatch, which relays a special from Rome, nearly word for word (A1, A2), so they are one report, not two independent ones.

accounts.label: Montgomery wire report (special from Rome)
accounts.gist: Martin, accused of assaulting a white woman, was captured and shot by a citizen posse, handed to a deputy sheriff to be taken to Florida, and taken from the officer before leaving Alabama, shot and thrown into a well; the report says he had confessed.

framing.detail: Headlined 'A Brutal Negro's End' in Kansas, the dispatch treated the assault and a 'full confession' as fact and named no killers (A2); the Atlanta Constitution ran it as a routine item in its Alabama news column (A1).

conflicts.note: Small wording difference in the same dispatch; both name a single deputy sheriff earlier.
